Restates the research question and describes dataset scope (146,028 dyads, 4 leagues, 2012-13 season).

spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is supported
the adjusted risk difference between dark- and light-skinned players is 0.28 percentage points (95% CI 0.03 to 0.56, p=0.024), a 23% relative increase
the adjusted odds ratio for red cards is 1.242 (95% CI 1.027 to 1.502, p=0.025) for dark- vs light-skinned players
the absolute effect size is modest but statistically significant and meaningful given the low (1.2%) base rate of red cards
the finding suggests implicit or explicit bias based on perceived skin tone may influence referee decisions, even after accounting for position, league, exposure, and yellow cards
the adjusted risk-difference point estimate is 0.2776pp (0.28pp), 95% CI [0.0309, 0.5573], two-sided p=0.0244
adjusted for number of games, player position, league country, and yellow cards received
after this adjustment, dark-skinned players (skin tone ≥0.75) show a 0.28pp higher absolute red-card risk than light-skinned players (≤0.25), with a 95% CI excluding zero (significant at α=0.05)
unadjusted red-card rate is 1.21% (light) vs 1.41% (dark); adjusted risk is 1.20% vs 1.48%; relative risk increase is 23.2%, equivalent to ~3 additional red cards per 1,000 dark-skinned dyads
the adjusted odds-ratio point estimate is 1.242, 95% CI [1.027, 1.502], two-sided p=0.0251
odds of a red card are 24.2% higher for dark-skinned than light-skinned players after adjustment; the CI narrowly excludes 1.0, consistent with the risk-difference finding
chose the player-referee dyad (full encounter history between one player and one referee) as the unit of analysis, reasoning referees may behave differently toward different players
final analysis sample is 100,135 dyads (84,050 light-skinned [83.9%], 16,085 dark-skinned [16.1%]), covering 1,227 unique players, 2,780 unique referees, and 1,243 total red cards (1.24% of dyads)
defined the outcome as a binary indicator for whether the player received any red card (direct or second-yellow) from that referee across all encounters
had two independent raters, blind to the research question, code each player's skin tone from profile photos on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was high: Pearson correlation 0.939, Spearman correlation 0.809
dichotomized skin tone into light (≤0.25) and dark (≥0.75) groups, excluding the middle range to maximize contrast and reduce measurement error from ambiguous classifications
adjusted for number of games in the dyad (continuous), reasoning it proxies exposure time
each additional game increases the odds of a red card by 12%, making games a strong predictor
adjusted for player position (5 categories), reasoning some positions involve more foul-prone contact
position distribution differs by skin tone: dark-skinned players are more likely to be forwards
adjusted for league country (4 categories), reasoning leagues may differ in officiating standards and player composition
dark-skinned players are more common in England/France, less common in Germany/Spain
adjusted for yellow cards received in the dyad (continuous), as a proxy for aggressive play or referee strictness
light-skinned players have slightly more yellow cards per dyad (0.41 vs 0.37) than dark-skinned players
fit a logistic regression of red card on dark skin, games, position, league, and yellow cards, with player-clustered robust standard errors
clustered standard errors by player to account for within-player correlation (~82 dyads per player on average), for conservative inference
did not additionally cluster standard errors by referee, due to computational complexity of crossed random effects
not clustering by referee may slightly underestimate uncertainty from referee-level variation, making the test slightly anticonservative

estimated the risk difference via marginal standardization (g-computation): fit the adjusted model, created counterfactual datasets setting dark skin to 1 and 0 for all observations, predicted probabilities under each, and took the difference in means
this g-computation approach properly accounts for covariate distributions and avoids non-collapsibility issues of odds ratios

computed the 95% CI by simulating 10,000 parameter vectors from the model's asymptotic multivariate normal distribution, calculating the risk difference for each, taking the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles, and deriving the two-sided p-value as 2×min(P(RD≥0),P(RD≤0))
this simulation approach properly propagates parameter uncertainty into the risk-difference estimate while accounting for clustering
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) with missing skin tone ratings (players without photos or unavailable ratings)
excluded 17,015 dyads (11.6%) with middle-range skin tones to create a clear light/dark contrast
excluded 7,471 dyads (5.1%) with missing player position, since position could not be adjusted for otherwise
total exclusions amounted to 45,893 dyads, 31.4% of the original data

spans.note: Caveat that excluded players may differ systematically, risking selection bias.
Caveat that excluding the middle range limits generalizability to the full skin-tone spectrum.

spans.assertion: a sensitivity analysis using a more inclusive skin-tone definition shows a smaller effect
averaged the two raters' skin-tone scores, then dichotomized into ≤0.25 vs ≥0.75
defined the red-card outcome as any red card (one or more)

spans.note: Notes results cannot be generalized to women's soccer.

spans.assertion: the unadjusted effect varies substantially by country: Germany +0.68pp and England +0.42pp (dark-skinned more likely), Spain -0.32pp and France -0.61pp (dark-skinned less likely)

the overall positive effect appears driven by Germany and England; the effect may not be uniform across contexts, possibly reflecting differing referee training, cultural attitudes, or player composition, raising generalizability questions about the pooled estimate

the effect is sensitive to where the dark/not-dark line is drawn, suggesting it may be strongest at the extremes, which weakens confidence in the finding's robustness
assumed data are missing at random (MAR) conditional on observed covariates

spans.note: Caveat that if missingness depends on skin tone and red-card risk beyond observed covariates, results may be biased.

spans.assertion: a large proportion (31%) of the data was excluded
unadjusted red card rate is 1.21% (light) vs 1.41% (dark), an unadjusted risk difference of 0.20pp versus 0.28pp adjusted

the adjusted effect is larger than the unadjusted effect, implying covariates were partially suppressing the association, opposite of what confounding-driven spuriousness would predict, supporting the finding
games per dyad: light-skinned 3.07 (SD 3.73) vs dark-skinned 2.97 (SD 3.53), light-skinned dyads having slightly more exposure
yellow cards per dyad: light-skinned 0.41 (SD 0.85) vs dark-skinned 0.38 (SD 0.75), suggesting light-skinned players are not less aggressive
dark-skinned players are disproportionately forwards (23% vs 12%) and under-represented as goalkeepers (2% vs 12%); forwards may have different foul patterns
dark-skinned players are more concentrated in England (38% vs 25%) and France (30% vs 11%), less so in Germany (19% vs 38%) and Spain (13% vs 26%)
substantial covariate imbalance exists, justifying the need for adjustment
the model's discrimination is good (AUC=0.740), distinguishing dyads with/without red cards better than chance
the model is well calibrated: mean predicted probability (1.24%) matches the observed rate exactly, with good calibration across deciles aside from typical over/under-prediction at the extremes

the top 10 referees gave 13-20 red cards each with no single referee dominating, and the correlation between a referee's exposure to dark-skinned players and total red cards is essentially zero (r=-0.011)
the effect is not driven by a few biased referees but is diffuse across many referees
games has OR=1.123 per game (+12% odds), the strongest predictor besides skin tone
yellow cards has OR=1.122 per card (+12% odds), confirming it captures playing style/referee strictness
relative to defenders, ORs are: Forward 0.705 (-30%), Goalkeeper 0.881 (-12%, n.s.), Midfielder 0.616 (-38%), Other 0.533 (-47%)
relative to England, ORs are: France 1.584 (+58%), Germany 0.964 (-4%, n.s.), Spain 1.633 (+63%)
France and Spain have higher overall red-card rates; position effects suggest defenders receive more red cards because defensive fouls are sanctioned more harshly
ran a sensitivity analysis using an alternative skin-tone cutoff of ≤0.375 vs ≥0.625
the more inclusive cutoff includes more players but yields weaker contrast; result OR=1.15, p=0.14 (not significant), suggesting the effect is stronger at the extremes
ran by-league subgroup analyses using unadjusted comparisons
by-league unadjusted effects: Germany +0.68pp (largest), England +0.42pp, Spain -0.32pp (opposite direction), France -0.61pp (opposite direction)
there is substantial heterogeneity across leagues; the pooled estimate may mask important variation
conducted all analyses using Python 3.11 with pandas, statsmodels, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, and matplotlib
set the random seed to 42 for all stochastic procedures (the simulation-based confidence intervals)
